faces.cost: Highest, and rarest: it runs on the people already found rather than on the whole picture.
faces.label: Who it is
faces.requires: Face recognition, which is off until you turn it on under Settings. While it is off this camera still reports that somebody is there - just not who.
faces.summary: When somebody is seen, compare their face against the people you have taught it. Everybody else is reported as a stranger.

motion.cost: Small. A couple of low-resolution frames a second, and none of the good stream.
motion.label: Movement
motion.summary: Polaris watches the small stream for movement, against what the view normally looks like - so a tree that sways all afternoon stops counting and somebody walking in does not. Use it when the camera cannot report its own movement, or reports far too much.

none.label: Nothing
none.summary: Watch it live, and record if you asked for that. Nothing is analyzed.

objects.cost: Moderate, and only while something is actually happening. Idle the rest of the time.
objects.label: People, vehicles and animals
objects.summary: When something moves, Polaris looks properly for as long as it is there, and says what it was and whereabouts in the picture. One arrival is one entry, with the clearest frame of it. This is what stops a swaying branch waking the house. It says a person is there, never which person - that is the rung below.

power.batteryCost: This camera is running off its own charge, and anything Polaris watches for itself means holding its stream open all day. That is a large increase in what it draws: if it is not recharging faster than that, it will run flat and switch itself off, and Polaris cannot wake it.

notes.battery: Polaris connects only while you are looking. It will not check on it and it will not watch for movement, because both of those mean holding the stream open, which is what empties the battery.
notes.battery-solar: The same as on a battery. A panel replaces what a day costs, not what a permanent connection costs, so nothing here holds one open.
notes.mains: Polaris treats it like any other camera: it keeps the picture up to date and tells you when it stops answering.

tapo.label: TP-Link Tapo (camera account)
tapo.note: In the Tapo app: Settings > Advanced > Camera Account. The account you create there is the one Polaris needs - your TP-Link login will not work.

tapo-battery.label: TP-Link Tapo (battery, no RTSP)
tapo-battery.note: For the ones with a battery in them - C400, C410, C420, C425, D230 - which publish no RTSP however they are configured. One of these is asleep almost all the time and answers nothing at all while it is: it wakes on its own movement, or when the Tapo app opens it. nuki-web.label: Nuki Web account
nuki-web.summary: One token for every lock on the account, and it answers from another country as readily as from the next room.
nuki-web.note: Everything goes through Nuki's own servers, so it is as reachable as they are and the state it reports is as recent as the last time a lock spoke to them. Checking again asks the locks themselves, which is why that is a button rather than a timer.

steps.s0: Open Nuki Web and sign in with the account the locks are on.
steps.s1: Under API, create a token that may see and operate your Smart Locks.
steps.s2: Paste it here. Nuki shows it once.

nuki-local.label: Nuki on your own network
nuki-local.summary: The locks talk to a broker in the building, so they answer in milliseconds and keep working when nobody's servers do.
nuki-local.note: This is the way in the newer locks actually have: a Smart Lock Pro, Ultra or Go has wifi of its own and no local web address at all, but it will publish itself to an MQTT broker on its own network. It costs the lock nothing to be read, so the state here is always current. What it cannot do is reach a lock from anywhere else, and it does not carry the account's record of who opened the door - the web account does both, and the two are worth having together. Nuki's firmware has no room for encryption, so this only ever runs unencrypted on a network you control, which is their rule rather than ours.

steps.s0: You need an MQTT broker running on the same network as the locks. Anything already running one - a smart-home hub, a Zigbee bridge - is the same broker.
steps.s1: In the Nuki app, open Device Administration then MQTT, switch it on and enter that broker's address and credentials.
steps.s2: Put the same address and credentials here.

host.label: Broker address
host.hint: A name or address on the same network as the locks. Nuki's firmware will not connect to anything outside it.

prefix.label: Topic prefix
prefix.hint: What the locks publish under. Nuki's own default, unless you changed it.

mqtt-discovery.label: A broker on your own network
mqtt-discovery.summary: Every switch, plug and light that announces itself on your broker, whatever made it - one connection instead of one per brand.
mqtt-discovery.note: Zigbee2MQTT, Tasmota, ESPHome, Shelly and anything written against them publish a description of each device alongside its state, and this reads those. Nothing here talks to Home Assistant or needs it installed; the convention is what is being read, and a broker that has one on it is simply a broker with these topics on it. Things that are on or off and things that lock arrive; sensors, blinds and thermostats announce themselves the same way and are left out until Polaris can draw them honestly.

steps.s0: You need an MQTT broker on the same network, which anything publishing devices this way already has.
steps.s1: Switch discovery on in whatever publishes them. It is on by default in Zigbee2MQTT and Tasmota.
steps.s2: Put the broker's address and credentials here.

host.label: Broker address
host.hint: A name or address Polaris can reach on this network.

prefix.label: Discovery prefix
prefix.hint: What the descriptions are published under. The convention's own default, unless you changed it.

tuya-app.label: Smart Life / Tuya Smart app
tuya-app.summary: Sign in by scanning a code with the app your devices are already in. No developer account.
tuya-app.note: It reaches every home on the app account through Tuya's servers. The sign-in renews itself, and removing this connection signs Polaris out at Tuya as well.

steps.s0: In the Smart Life or Tuya Smart app, open Me, tap the gear, then Account and Security.
steps.s1: Copy the User Code shown at the bottom and paste it below.
steps.s2: Scan the code Polaris shows with the same app: tap + or Add Device, then Scan.

userCode.label: User Code from the app
userCode.hint: Shown under Account and Security in the app. It is not your password.

pairing.prompt: In the Smart Life or Tuya Smart app, tap + or Add Device, choose Scan and point it at this code.

tuya-cloud.label: Tuya cloud project
tuya-cloud.summary: Everything on the Smart Life or Tuya app account, whatever brand is printed on it: switches, sockets and lights.
tuya-cloud.note: Tuya is what is inside a few thousand makes, so a plug with somebody else's name on the box is usually this. The keys come from their developer console, which is free, and the app account has to be linked to the project there - keys that work while the account is not linked are the one way this goes wrong quietly, so Polaris says so rather than showing an empty list.

steps.s0: Open the Tuya IoT console and create a cloud project, choosing the data center your app account is in.
steps.s1: On the project's Devices tab, link the Smart Life or Tuya app account your devices are on.
steps.s2: Copy the Access ID and Access Secret from the project overview.

accessSecret.label: Access Secret
accessSecret.placeholder: Shown next to the Access ID

region.label: Data center
region.hint: The one the project was created in. Devices exist in that one only, so anywhere else answers as though the account were empty.

tapo-local.label: Tapo on your own network
tapo-local.summary: A plug, strip, switch or bulb answered directly at its address, with the account you use in the Tapo app.
tapo-local.note: Nothing goes through TP-Link's servers, so it answers in milliseconds and keeps working when their cloud does not. One connection is one device: a strip brings in each of its outlets. Plugs on very old Tapo firmware use an earlier handshake Polaris does not speak; updating them in the Tapo app fixes that.

steps.s0: Find the device's IP address in your router's list of connected devices. Giving it a fixed address there keeps this working.
steps.s1: Use the email and password you sign into the Tapo app with.

host.label: Device address
host.hint: On the same network as Polaris.

email.label: TP-Link email
email.placeholder: The one you use in the Tapo app

kasa-local.label: Kasa on your own network
kasa-local.summary: An older Kasa plug, strip or bulb, answered directly at its address. Most need no account.
kasa-local.note: Kasa devices on older firmware answer anyone on the network, so the address is enough. Newer firmware asks for the TP-Link account, the same one as the Kasa app. One connection is one device: a strip brings in each of its outlets.

steps.s0: Find the device's IP address in your router's list of connected devices, and give it a fixed one there if you can.
steps.s1: If Polaris says the device refused, add the email and password you use in the Kasa app.

host.label: Device address
host.hint: On the same network as Polaris.

email.label: TP-Link email
email.hint: Only for newer firmware. Leave empty otherwise.

shelly-local.label: Shelly on your own network
shelly-local.summary: A Shelly relay, plug, dimmer or bulb, answered directly at its address. No account needed.
shelly-local.note: Every Shelly, old or new, answers on its own network, so nothing goes through a cloud and it keeps working without the internet. One connection is one Shelly: each relay or light channel on it becomes a row. Blinds and meters are left out for now.

steps.s0: Find the Shelly's IP address in your router's list of connected devices, and give it a fixed one there if you can.
steps.s1: If you set a password on it in the Shelly app, add it here.

host.label: Device address
host.hint: On the same network as Polaris.

password.label: Password
password.hint: Only if you turned on authentication for this Shelly.

username.label: Username
username.hint: Only older Shelly devices use one, and it is admin unless you changed it.

hue-bridge.label: Hue Bridge
hue-bridge.summary: Every light and smart plug on your Hue Bridge, from one press of its button. Nothing goes through the cloud.
hue-bridge.note: Polaris talks to the bridge on your network and checks its certificate against Hue's own, so it answers in milliseconds and keeps working without the internet. Lights and plugs arrive; scenes, rooms and colours stay in the Hue app.

steps.s0: Find the bridge's IP address in your router's list of connected devices.
steps.s1: Press the link button on the bridge.

host.label: Bridge address
host.hint: On the same network as Polaris.

appKey.label: Application key
appKey.hint: Leave it empty and Polaris makes one when you press the bridge's button.

dirigera-hub.label: DIRIGERA hub
dirigera-hub.summary: The lights, outlets and sensors on your IKEA DIRIGERA hub, from one press of its button. Nothing goes through the cloud.
dirigera-hub.note: Polaris talks to the hub on your network. The hub's certificate is remembered when you pair it, and Polaris refuses to talk to anything else at that address afterwards. Blinds, air purifiers and remotes are left out for now.

steps.s0: Find the hub's IP address in your router, and give it a fixed one if you can.
steps.s2: Within a minute, press the action button on the hub.

host.label: Hub address
host.hint: On the same network as Polaris.

home-assistant.label: Home Assistant
home-assistant.summary: Every switch, light, lock and sensor your Home Assistant already has, from one connection.
home-assistant.note: Whatever Home Assistant talks to arrives through it: Zigbee, Z-Wave and its cloud integrations included. Polaris reads states and sends the same on, off, lock and unlock you would press there. Blinds, thermostats and media players are left out for now.

steps.s0: In Home Assistant, open your profile page.
steps.s1: Under Long-lived access tokens, create one called Polaris and copy it. It is shown once.
steps.s2: Paste it here with the address you open Home Assistant at.

url.label: Home Assistant address
url.hint: The one you open it at. Port 8123 is assumed if you give only an address.

switchbot-cloud.label: SwitchBot account
switchbot-cloud.summary: Plugs, Bots, locks, lights and sensors on your SwitchBot account, reachable from anywhere.
switchbot-cloud.note: Everything goes through SwitchBot's servers, so Bluetooth devices need a SwitchBot Hub. The account allows 10,000 requests a day, so the state shown here can be a few minutes old until you refresh. Curtains, humidifiers and infrared remotes are left out for now.

steps.s0: Open the SwitchBot app, then Profile > Preferences > About.
steps.s1: Tap the app version ten times until Developer Options appears.
steps.s2: Open Developer Options, tap Get Token, and copy the token and the secret key here.

connections.tooShort: That looks too short to be the {field}
connections.tooLong: That is longer than the {field} can be
connections.pickListed: Pick one of the listed options

gree-local.label: Gree+ (local network)
gree-local.summary: The air conditioners you use with the Gree+ app, straight over your network. No account, nothing through the cloud.
gree-local.note: Polaris finds the units on your network and pairs with each one, the way Home Assistant does. They have to be set up in the Gree+ app first, and on the same network as Polaris.

steps.s0: Set the air conditioner up in the Gree+ app, on the same Wi-Fi network as Polaris.
steps.s1: Pick a unit from the list, type its IP or MAC, or leave the address empty to pair every unit.

host.label: Unit address
host.hint: Optional. Empty pairs every unit found. The Gree+ app shows each unit's MAC.

philips-coap.label: Philips Air+ (local network)
philips-coap.summary: The air purifiers and humidifiers you use with the Philips Air+ app, straight over your network. No account, nothing through the cloud.
philips-coap.note: Polaris finds the units on your network and reads them the way Home Assistant does. They have to be set up in the Philips Air+ app first, on the same network as Polaris or on one your router connects to it. Some newer firmware switches local control off; such a unit may work through a Philips Air+ account instead, and Polaris says so.

steps.s0: Set the purifier up in the Philips Air+ app, on the same Wi-Fi network as Polaris.
steps.s1: Select Connect. Leave the address empty to look for every unit, or type one to add just that unit.

host.label: Unit address
host.hint: Optional. Empty looks for every unit on this network; your router lists each unit's address among its connected devices. A unit on another network is only found by its address.

philips-cloud.label: Philips account
philips-cloud.summary: The air purifiers, fans and kitchen appliances on your Philips account, through Philips' cloud like its apps. Works from any network.
philips-cloud.note: Unofficial: Philips publishes no API for this, so it could stop working if Philips changes its cloud. It signs in with a code Philips emails you, and no password is kept. Purifier models it knows: AC0650, AC0651, AC1715, AC3221, AC3360, AC4220 and AC4221, and the CX3550 fan; others show their readings and power only. Kitchen appliances are shown, never started; an airfryer can be stopped. Fans and heaters need the Philips Air+ app file once. If a purifier is on the same network as Polaris, the local connection does not depend on Philips.

steps.s0: Set the device up in its Philips app (Air+, HomeID or NutriU) and sign in there with your email.
steps.s1: Pick your country, type that email and select Email me a code. Philips sends you a one-time code.
steps.s2: Type the code here. Polaris lists the devices on the account, and asks for the Philips Air+ app file if it needs it.

country.label: Country or region
country.hint: The one your Philips account is set up in. Philips keeps each country's devices in one region.

email.label: Email
email.hint: The one you sign in to the Philips app with.

pairing.prompt: Philips has emailed a one-time code to that address. It can take a minute to arrive; check spam too.

file.title: Upload the Philips Air+ app file (.apk)
file.why: Polaris asked Philips' servers for {country} ({area}) and every other region it knows, and no Air+ or HomeID list holds an air device ({summary}). Fans, heaters and some purifiers are on a third Philips cloud, which only accepts sign-ins signed with a value Philips keeps inside its Air+ app. Polaris reads that value from the file without running it, keeps it encrypted with this connection and deletes the file.
file.homeid: Philips' HomeID service failed on this account. If the device is in the HomeID app, removing it there and adding it again usually fixes that.
file.where: Download it (com.philips.ph.homecare) from APKMirror in your browser; any version works.

philips-cloud.foundIn: Found on Philips' servers in {found}, not in {asked}, where accounts from {country} usually are. Polaris will keep using {found}.

connections.macReserved: That is not a device's MAC address.

settings.footageBody: Recordings and the pictures that go with events are written to {storage}. That is set for the whole instance under Uploads, beside where photos and attachments go - one place for one decision. A camera that wants its own disk says so on its own settings.
settings.sensitivityBody: Nobody guesses these right the first time, and they are not the same for a hallway and a garden facing a hedge. Set them once here, from the camera you have already tuned, and every camera added afterwards starts there. Each camera can still disagree.
settings.settleHint: Seconds. This is the one that stops moths, gusts and passing lorries: nearly every false alarm is over within a second or two, and a person is not.
settings.gapHint: Seconds. Somebody standing at a door is one thing that happened, not sixty.
settings.facesBody: Off unless you turn it on. It puts names to the people you have taught it under People, and only after a camera has already seen somebody - the pictures and what is learned from them stay on the machine it runs on. While it is on it holds its models in memory, so leave it off if you only want cameras to say that somebody is there.
settings.offButRunningHint: Nothing is asking it anything. Stopping it gives back the memory it holds its models in; turning recognition back on starts it again.
settings.offHint: Cameras report that somebody is there, and never who. Nothing is running for it.
settings.installHint: A few hundred megabytes, once. It runs on the processor - no graphics card needed.
settings.noneYet: Until there is one, cameras set to recognize faces still report that somebody is there - just not who.
settings.sensitivityTitle: How sensitive a new camera is
settings.runningHint: Teach it who lives here under People, and cameras set to recognize faces will start using their names.
settings.waitedHint: It has had several minutes and has not come up. The machine may be busy pulling it down, or the container may have stopped - it is under Apps, by the name it was installed with.
settings.startingHint: It loads its models the first time it starts, which takes a minute or two. Nothing is lost in the meantime - cameras still report that somebody is there.

clips.emptyBody: A camera keeps footage once you tell it to, on its own settings screen.
clips.deleteBody: The file is removed from wherever it was written. There is no copy.

events.emptyBody: When a camera notices something, it turns up here with the picture it took.
events.noFootage: No footage of this moment was kept
events.deleteAllBody: Everything the current filters match is removed, along with its pictures. Footage is not touched.

zones.corners: {count} corners. Drag one to move it.

watch.label: Watch this area
watch.summary: Only what happens inside counts. Draw more than one and any of them will do.

ignore.label: Ignore this area
ignore.summary: Nothing here is ever reported. The road, the pavement, the tree that moves all afternoon.

zones.title: Areas on {name}
zones.intro: Draw the parts of the picture that matter. Click the frame to place each corner. Until you draw one, the whole picture counts.
zones.none: None yet, so everything this camera sees counts.
zones.rest: Anything else here is treated as if the area were not drawn.
zones.noPicture: No picture from this camera right now. You can still draw on the frame - an area is a fraction of the picture, not a set of pixels.

alerts.intro: Everything the cameras see is in Events either way. An alert is what you want telling about: it arrives as a message in a conversation with the people you pick.

kinds.package: A box or bag is left

alerts.undrawn: A camera nobody has drawn on will never match this.
alerts.notify: Also send it to their notifications
alerts.notifyOn: It reaches the bell as well, and wherever each person sends their alerts. Everyone chooses that in their own notification settings.
alerts.notifyOff: Only the conversation. Nothing lands on the bell.

alerts.readFailed: Your alerts could not be read. Reload the page to try again.
alerts.extrasFailed: The faces and areas an alert can name could not be read, so alerts cannot be added or changed. Reload the page to try again.
alerts.emptyBody: Everything the cameras see is kept in Events. An alert is for the few things worth being told about: it arrives as a message in a conversation with the people you choose.
alerts.removeBody: Nobody is told about this again. The conversation it wrote into stays - what it holds actually happened.

qualityHints.moderate: Keep the purifier on and the windows shut.
qualityHints.poor: Keep it on, turn it up and keep the windows shut.

qualityHints.extremelyPoor: Run it on turbo and stay out of the room if you can.

devicesView.unreachable: {name} could not be reached, so its devices are as they were when it last answered.

devicesView.emptyManage: Connect what your locks, switches and lights are on and they appear here, with their state, their controls and everything they have done.
devicesView.emptyView: Somebody who administers Places can connect what the devices are on.
devicesView.nothingBody: Check that this is the account the devices are on, and that what it was connected with may see them.

devicePanel.watchOnly: Set to be watched rather than operated.
devicePanel.batteryLow: The battery is nearly flat. Once it runs out it stops answering, and whatever it does has to be done by hand.

devicePanel.noControl: You can see this, but not operate it.
devicePanel.offline: It is not answering, so it cannot be switched now.

deviceDialog.readBack: Everything else about it is read back from that account.
deviceDialog.areaHint: Doors and cameras in the same area are shown together.
deviceDialog.operateHint: Off leaves the state and the history and takes away the buttons.

connect.search: Search for a make or a device

discover.fromHint: For a camera on a network Polaris cannot reach - another building, a guest network, the far side of a repeater. That machine does the looking.

people.addIntro: Their name, and a few photographs of their face. Without photographs the cameras still see them - they are just reported as a stranger.
people.photosHint: Four or five, in different light, one face per photograph. One photograph recognizes that photograph; several recognize a person.
people.facesOff: Face recognition is off, so there is nowhere to send them. Turn it on under Settings - the name can be written down now and starts working then.
people.noRecognizer: Nothing is recognizing faces yet. Names written here start working the moment something is.
people.emptyBody: Add the people who live here with a few photographs each, and the cameras stop reporting them as strangers.
people.noPhotos: No photographs yet - they will still be reported as a stranger
people.fewHint: A few photographs recognize a person; one recognizes a photograph
people.forgetBody: Their photographs are deleted from the recognizer as well. The cameras will report them as a stranger from then on.

reasons.disabled: Stopped because it was switched off.
reasons.edited: Stopped because its steps were changed while it ran.
reasons.timedOut: Stopped: the device did not get there in time.
reasons.step: Stopped at the step that failed.
reasons.fault: Something went wrong running it. Nothing after that step ran.
reasons.unreadable: This automation was saved by a newer Polaris and could not be read, so nothing ran.

notes.deviceGone: That device is no longer here.

notes.automationHeld: That automation was not started: it ran too many times in the last few minutes, or this step had already started it.
notes.toggleUnknown: Its state was not known, so there was nothing to switch over.
